raw.answer: The case asked whether the control power (監察權) can be exercised over the speakers of provincial and county councils. The court decided it cannot, because a speaker is still an elected council representative. If a speaker handles council affairs improperly, the council itself should discipline the speaker.
raw.held: Provincial and county council speakers are not public officials under Article 97, paragraph 2 and Article 98 of the Constitution, so the control power does not apply to them. Improper handling of council affairs is for the council itself to sanction.

points.text: Elected representatives are not subjects of the control power, as already stated in Interpretation No. 14.
Provincial and county councils are representative bodies, and their speakers are chosen by the councillors from among themselves.
Although a speaker is responsible for handling council affairs, the speaker's status as a representative does not change.
So a speaker is not a public official within the meaning of Article 97, paragraph 2 and Article 98 of the Constitution.
Any improper conduct in handling council affairs should be sanctioned by the council itself.

raw.answer: The case asked what a court should do when someone commits repeated offenses and the charges end up in different courts. In the example, a person stole in one county and was prosecuted there, then stole in a second county. The ruling said the second county's court may take both cases together, and once its judgment is final, the first court must dismiss the earlier case without a trial on the merits.
raw.held: Article 8 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not apply to the later theft, which was never before the first court. The second county's court, as the defendant's location court, may combine the earlier unjudged offense under Article 5, and after its final judgment the first court must issue a dismissal (免訴) under Article 294, item 1.

points.text: Article 8 mainly aims to stop several courts that each have jurisdiction from trying the same case.
The theft in the second county was never before the first county's court, so Article 8 does not come into play.
The second county's court is the court where the defendant is located, so under Article 5 it may take the earlier, still-untried offense along with the new one.
Once the second court's judgment is final, the first court must dismiss the earlier prosecution under Article 294, item 1.

who: Defendants accused of repeated offenses in different places
Courts in different counties handling related charges

raw.answer: The case asked whether an innocent third party can claim a debt against property that an enforcement agency has lawfully confiscated in a special criminal case. The court said the agency does not automatically have to pay the convicted person's debts. But an uninformed third party with a validly created debt claim can make that claim, and it is handled under the compulsory enforcement rules.
raw.held: The enforcement agency is not automatically responsible for repaying the convicted person's debts from confiscated property. If a third party who did not know of the crime has a lawfully created claim and asserts it, the matter is handled under the relevant provisions of the Compulsory Enforcement Act, as Article 475 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides.

points.text: Confiscating property in a special criminal case does not by itself make the enforcement agency liable for the convicted person's debts.
The spirit of Article 15 of the Constitution, which protects people's property rights, supports letting an uninformed third party assert a lawfully created claim.
Under Article 475 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, such a claim is to be handled under the relevant provisions of the Compulsory Enforcement Act.

who: Innocent third parties holding debt claims
Persons convicted in special criminal cases

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Control Yuan's power of oversight can be used against legislators, Control Yuan members, National Assembly delegates, and provincial or county councilors. The court decided it cannot, because these people are elected representatives and the framers did not intend them to be targets of that power. Other staff of the Legislative and Control Yuans, National Assembly employees, and Presidential Office staff do fall within it.
raw.held: Legislators, Control Yuan members, National Assembly delegates, and provincial and county council members are not subject to the Control Yuan's oversight power. Other staff of the two Yuans, National Assembly employees, and Presidential Office and affiliated agency staff are within it.

points.text: Articles 97, 98 and 99 of the Constitution came from draft articles 102, 103 and 104, which covered impeachment of executive officials, central and local administrative staff, and judges and Examination Yuan staff.

At the constitution-making assembly, proposals to extend impeachment to Legislative and Control Yuan members were not passed, showing they were meant to be excluded; reading 'central public servants' to include them would be hard to justify.

The framers saw legislators and Control Yuan members as direct or indirect representatives of the people, so not objects of oversight, while other staff of those Yuans, National Assembly staff and Presidential Office staff are covered.
National Assembly delegates are people's representatives, and no draft or amendment proposed impeaching them, consistent with the framers' consistent intent.
Members of provincial and county councils are also people's representatives, so by the same reasoning they are not subject to oversight.

raw.answer: The case asked what kind of penalty the fines under the Stamp Tax Act are, and whether a person must have acted intentionally to be fined. The court decided the fines are purely administrative penalties, and that a violation does not require intent. It also changed an earlier interpretation (院字第一四六四號).
raw.held: Fines under the Stamp Tax Act are purely administrative penalties. A taxpayer who has committed a violation is to be fined according to how serious it is, and intent is not required. Earlier interpretation 院字第一四六四號 is changed.

points.text: The fines set by the Stamp Tax Act are purely administrative penalties.
Where a taxpayer has violated the law, a fine must be imposed under the law, with the amount depending on how serious the circumstances are.
A violation does not depend on intent, so intent is not an element of the offense.
The earlier interpretation 院字第一四六四號 addressed a specific situation at that time, so it is changed.

who: Taxpayers under the Stamp Tax Act
Authorities imposing Stamp Tax Act fines

raw.answer: The case asked whether a woman's adopted daughter and the woman's own adopted son may marry each other. The court decided they may not, because they are artificial blood relatives of different generations, and it said an earlier interpretation (No. 12) does not apply here.
raw.held: A mother's adopted daughter and her own adopted son may not marry, under Article 983, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Civil Code. Interpretation No. 12 differs from this situation and cannot be relied on.

points.text: The two are artificial blood relatives whose generations (rank) differ.
Under Article 983, paragraph 1, item 2 of the Civil Code, such relatives cannot marry.
Interpretation No. 12 concerns a different situation, so it cannot be applied here.

who: Adopted sons of the same mother

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the Legislative Yuan may also serve as a member of the National Assembly. The court decided that they may not, because the two roles are incompatible and holding both conflicts with the spirit of the Constitution.
raw.held: Legislative Yuan members may not concurrently serve as National Assembly delegates.

points.text: Article 75 of the Constitution only bars legislators from being officials, but that does not mean any other post is allowed; each post must be checked for compatibility with a legislator's duties.
Under Article 27, the National Assembly votes on constitutional amendments proposed by the Legislative Yuan, so one person would be both proposer and decider, which are incompatible roles.
A legislator already exercises legislative power, and also taking part in initiating and referring national laws for a public vote would conflict with the spirit of Articles 25 and 62.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the wartime regulation protecting transport equipment applies when a railway's equipment is stolen in wartime. The court said it does for railways built and run by public or private businesses that in practice carry public transport duties and are supervised by the transport authority. It said light tracks (commonly called handcart lines) are different from ordinary railways and are not covered.
raw.held: Equipment stolen in wartime from a public or private business's railway that in fact bears public transport responsibility and is supervised by the transport authority falls under the wartime transport equipment protection regulation. Light tracks (handcart lines) are not covered.

points.text: The railway in question was laid by a public or private business but in fact carries public transport responsibility.
It is also under the supervision and management of the transport authority, so theft of its equipment in wartime can be dealt with under the wartime regulation.
Light tracks (handcart lines) differ from ordinary railways, so the regulation cannot be extended to them.

who: Public and private businesses that operate railways
People accused of stealing railway equipment in wartime

raw.answer: The case asked whether elected representatives and similar officeholders count as holding a "public office" (公職) under Article 18 of the Constitution. The court decided that the term is broad and includes them. The ruling gives no further detail or reasoning.
raw.held: The court held that "public office" in Article 18 has a broad meaning. It covers all levels of elected representatives, civil servants in central and local government bodies, and others who perform public duties according to law.

points.text: The question was whether elected representatives at various levels and similar personnel hold "public office" under Article 18.
The court said "public office" in Article 18 is very broad in meaning.
It listed who is covered: representatives at all levels, civil servants of central and local bodies, and others who perform public duties under law.

who: Others performing public duties under law

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the Control Yuan (a 監察委員) may also serve as a National Assembly delegate. The court decided they may not hold both roles at once, because the two roles conflict under the Constitution.
raw.held: A Control Yuan member may not also serve as a National Assembly delegate.

points.text: National Assembly delegates exercise political power on behalf of the people, so the post is a public office. Article 103 of the Constitution bars Control Yuan members from holding other public offices.

Articles 100 and 27 split the powers over the President and Vice President: the Control Yuan impeaches, and the National Assembly recalls. One person holding both posts would exercise both powers, which goes against the Constitution's original intent to divide them.

The draft Constitution's Article 26 first allowed legislators and Control Yuan members to be delegates. After many delegates objected and proposed amendments, the Constitutional Assembly deleted those two items on the review committee's advice, which supports the view that holding both is not allowed.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a contract that pays rent in goods instead of money breaks the Civil Code's rules on leases. The court decided that agreeing to pay rent in white rice does not conflict with Article 421, paragraph 2 of the Civil Code. The ruling does not give detailed reasons beyond this.
raw.held: An agreement between the parties to pay housing rent in white rice does not conflict with Article 421, paragraph 2 of the Civil Code. Unless other laws specifically forbid it, the law does not prohibit it.

points.text: The question was whether paying rent in goods rather than money violates the Civil Code's lease rules.
Paying rent in white rice by agreement of both parties does not conflict with Article 421, paragraph 2 of the Civil Code.
Such an agreement is permitted unless some other law specifically forbids it.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a business counts as state-owned when a state-owned enterprise has put in more than half of its capital. The court decided that money a state-owned enterprise invests in another business is treated as government capital. If that money is more than 50% of the other business's capital, the other business is a state-owned enterprise under the law the ruling names.
raw.held: Funds that a state-owned enterprise invests in another business count as government capital. If they exceed 50% of that business's capital, it is a state-owned enterprise under Article 3, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the State-Owned Enterprise Management Act.

points.text: The question was whether a business is state-owned when a state-owned enterprise has invested more than half of its capital.
Money that a state-owned enterprise reinvests in other businesses is to be treated as government capital.
If that money is more than 50% of the other business's capital, the business is a state-owned enterprise under Article 3, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the State-Owned Enterprise Management Act.

who: Businesses that state-owned enterprises invest in

raw.answer: The case asked whether legislators (members of the Legislative Yuan) and control members (members of the Control Yuan) hold paid public offices. The court decided that they do, because they exercise powers the Constitution gives them and receive regular pay and public allowances under the law.
raw.held: Legislative Yuan members and Control Yuan members hold public office, and because they lawfully receive annual pay and public allowances, they are to be treated as holding paid positions.

points.text: Legislators and control members exercise, in accordance with the law, powers that the Constitution gives them, so their positions are public offices.
They lawfully receive annual pay and public allowances, so their positions should be regarded as paid.

raw.answer: The case asked whether an item that a court has legally ordered confiscated is affected when the main sentence is given a suspended (probation) sentence. The court decided that confiscated items are not affected by the suspension, so the confiscation still stands.
raw.held: Confiscation of items ordered under the law is not affected by a suspended sentence on the main penalty.

points.text: An earlier interpretation (院字第七八一號) said a suspended main sentence also reaches secondary penalties, but this does not settle the matter for confiscation.

The law allows confiscation as the only penalty (Article 39) and allows confiscation to be ordered on its own (Article 40), showing confiscation, though a secondary penalty, is not necessarily tied to the main sentence.
Confiscated items are either ones the law requires be confiscated, or ones that may be confiscated and were found necessary to confiscate.

Such confiscation does not fit the purpose of a suspended sentence under Article 74, which is for cases where not carrying out the sentence for now is appropriate, so it is not affected by the suspension.

who: People whose property is ordered confiscated

raw.answer: The case asked whether the word 'judge' in the Constitution includes prosecutors, and whether prosecutors who hold a permanent post get the same protection as permanent judges. The court said 'judge' in Article 81 means the judges referred to in Article 80 and does not include prosecutors. It added that permanent prosecutors have the same protection as permanent judges, except when it comes to being transferred. The ruling as quoted gives no further reasoning.
raw.held: The 'judge' in Article 81 of the Constitution does not include prosecutors. Under Article 82 and Article 40, paragraph 2 of the Court Organization Act, permanent prosecutors are protected the same as permanent judges, except for transfers.

points.text: The 'judge' in Article 81 means the judge in Article 80 of the Constitution, so prosecutors are not included.
Permanent prosecutors are protected like permanent judges under Article 82 of the Constitution and Article 40, paragraph 2 of the Court Organization Act, but transfers are an exception.

raw.answer: The case asked whether, after the Constitution came into force, people who handle party affairs for political parties count as public officials under the criminal law. The court decided they do not. The paragraphs given do not set out the court's reasons.
raw.held: Staff who handle party affairs for the political parties after the Constitution took effect cannot be regarded as public officials as the criminal law uses that term.
who: Political party staff who handle party affairs

raw.answer: The case asked what prosecutors should do when a crime that can only be prosecuted on a victim's complaint has an invalid complaint, and whether a valid complaint can later lead to prosecution. The court said the prosecutor should decline to prosecute when the complaint is invalid or was filed by someone not legally allowed to complain. If another person with the right to complain later files a valid complaint, prosecution may go ahead.
raw.held: If a complaint is invalid or filed by someone not allowed to file it, the prosecutor must issue a non-prosecution decision under Article 234, paragraph 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. After such a decision, a valid complaint by another person entitled to complain allows prosecution, free of the limit in Article 239.

points.text: For complaint-only crimes, an invalid complaint or one filed by someone not legally allowed to complain requires a non-prosecution decision under Article 234, paragraph 1.

If no complaint was made at all, there is no decision to make. The part of Interpretation Yuan-Tzu No. 2292 to be changed refers only to invalid complaints and complaints filed by people not allowed to file.

After a non-prosecution decision based on an invalid complaint, another person with the right to complain may file a valid complaint, and prosecution is then allowed without the restriction in Article 239.

who: People who file complaints in complaint-only crimes
People with the legal right to complain

raw.answer: The case asked whether certain positions count as a "public office" (公職) under Article 103 of the Constitution. The court said heads and board members of party branches and women's work committees do not hold public office, but medical personnel, including directors and doctors of public hospitals, fall within the Article 103 restriction.
raw.held: Chairs and directors of the provincial party branch and the provincial women's work committee are not 'public office' under Article 103. Medical practitioners fall under the 'business' covered by that article, and public hospital directors and doctors also hold public office, so all of them are within its restriction.

points.text: The provincial party branch and the provincial women's work committee are people's organizations, so their chairs and directors are not public office under Article 103.

Medical personnel must obtain a certificate to practice and are regularly supervised by the competent authority, so their work is incompatible with the supervisory (監察) office's powers and counts as the 'business' named in Article 103.
Public hospitals are national or local medical agencies, so their directors and doctors also hold public office and are covered by the restriction.

who: Party branch and women's committee chairs and directors

raw.answer: The case asked how to fix a criminal judgment that names the wrong defendant, where the court wrote 'Zhang San' but meant 'Zhang Si'. The court said the remedy depends on whether a separate person named Zhang Si exists among those involved in the case. If one does, the judgment is unlawful and must be corrected through appeal, extraordinary appeal, or retrial; if not, it is treated as a simple writing slip that can be corrected.
raw.held: If a different person named Zhang Si exists in the case and was never prosecuted, the judgment violates the law and is fixed through appeal, extraordinary appeal or retrial. If no such person exists, it is a clerical error that can be corrected by the original court, by a ruling on request or on its own initiative once the judgment has been announced or served.

points.text: If another person with the mistaken name exists in the case and was not prosecuted, the judgment is contrary to law and is corrected through appeal, extraordinary appeal, or retrial as the situation requires.
If no such other person exists, the judgment does not match the Code of Criminal Procedure article 245 requirement and is plainly a writing mistake.
Such a writing mistake does not affect the facts of the whole case or the essential meaning of the judgment.
Before the judgment is announced, the error may be fixed by adding or deleting text under article 40 of the same Code.

After announcement or service, the original court may correct it by a ruling, on request or on its own authority, under article 199 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with reference to article 232 of the Code of Civil Procedure, to keep the matter careful and formal.

who: Criminal defendants named wrongly in a judgment
Persons wrongly named but not prosecuted

raw.answer: The case asked whether legislators and members of the Control Yuan may also serve as directors or supervisors of provincial banks. The court said they may not, because those bank posts count as public enterprise service positions. It also declined to answer several other points that had been submitted to it.
raw.held: Directors and supervisors of provincial banks are public enterprise personnel, so legislators and Control Yuan members cannot hold those posts at the same time. The court would not answer points one, three, four and five of the request because they did not meet its procedural rules.

points.text: Provincial bank directors and supervisors are all service personnel of public enterprise bodies.
Legislators and Control Yuan members cannot hold such positions, as already stated in the court's earlier Interpretation No. 24.

Points one, three, four and five of the request concern unifying the interpretation of laws, but the request did not explain how the views held differ from those of this or other bodies. This does not meet Article 4 of the Grand Justices Council rules, so the court could not answer them.

raw.answer: The case asked whether a public servant may also work as the publisher or editor of newspapers, magazines and similar publications. The court decided that, unless other laws provide otherwise, public servants may not hold those roles. The ruling gives no further reasoning in the paragraphs provided.
raw.held: Unless a law or regulation provides otherwise, a public servant may not serve as the publisher or editor of a newspaper-type publication or magazine, under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Civil Servants Service Act.

points.text: The question was whether public servants may concurrently serve as publishers or editors of newspapers and similar publications.
Under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Civil Servants Service Act, public servants cannot hold these posts, except where other laws or regulations say differently.

raw.answer: The Executive Yuan forwarded a request asking the Judicial Yuan to give a unified interpretation of a law. The court said an agency may seek a unified interpretation only in limited situations, and here the requesting agency had not shown it was in one, so the court declined to interpret.
raw.held: The court would not give an interpretation, because the requesting agency did not explain that its view of the same law differed from a view already expressed by its own or another agency.

points.text: The Constitution uses different wording for the Judicial Yuan's powers: it 'interprets' the Constitution but gives 'unified interpretation' of laws and orders, so the two powers differ in meaning.
Central or local agencies may ask for an interpretation when they doubt how to apply the Constitution, or whether a law or order conflicts with it.
For other doubts about applying a law or order, the agency that applies it must study it and decide its meaning itself, so there is no reason to let it ask the Judicial Yuan.

A unified interpretation is needed only when an agency's view differs from a view already expressed by its own or another agency on the same law, and it is not bound by that view or able to change its own.
The Executive Yuan's request did not state that the original agency's view differed from one already expressed by its own or another agency, so no interpretation was given.

who: Agencies applying the same law or order

raw.answer: The case asked whether the National Assembly, when it meets in a regular session, may use the powers that belong to its special (temporary) sessions. The court said that the powers used in a special session called under Article 30 of the Constitution are still part of the National Assembly's powers, so an assembly convened under Article 29 may use them.
raw.held: A National Assembly convened under Article 29 may exercise the powers it would use in a special session called under one of the situations listed in Article 30, because those powers are still part of the National Assembly's powers.

points.text: The question was whether a regular session of the National Assembly may exercise the powers of a special session.
The powers exercised when a special session is called under a situation listed in Article 30 are still one part of the National Assembly's powers.
Because of that, an assembly convened under Article 29 may exercise those powers.

raw.answer: The case asked whether people who work for government-run enterprises count as public officials under the criminal law. The court said that a company limited by shares in which the government holds more than 50 percent is a government-run enterprise, even if it is organized under the company law. People who carry out that company's duties under law are therefore public officials for criminal law purposes.
raw.held: A company limited by shares with government ownership above 50 percent is a government-run enterprise, and people who perform its duties under laws and orders are to be treated as public officials under the criminal law.

points.text: The question was whether staff of government-run enterprises are public officials under the criminal law.
A company limited by shares with more than 50 percent government shareholding is a government-run enterprise, even if it is organized under the company law.
Because of this, people who perform that company's duties under laws and orders are to be regarded as public officials in the criminal law sense.

raw.answer: The case asked whether someone who sells meat from illegally slaughtered cattle, stamped with a forged tax stamp, commits the crime of using a forged official document. The court said yes: a tax stamp placed on goods to show tax was paid counts as a document, and using a forged one this way is that crime.
raw.held: A tax authority's stamp placed on goods to prove tax payment is treated as a document. Selling illegally slaughtered beef marked with a forged tax stamp is the crime of using a forged official document, punished under Article 211 of the Criminal Code.

points.text: Under Article 220 of the Criminal Code, a tax authority's stamp placed on goods to prove tax payment is to be treated as a document.
Using a forged tax stamp on one's own illegally slaughtered beef to sell it meets Article 216, the offense of using a forged official document, and is handled under Article 211.
The word for 'seal' in the earlier Interpretation Yuan-Jie No. 3364's phrase on official-seal documents is taken to be superfluous text.

who: People who sell meat with forged tax stamps

raw.answer: The case asked whether a party to a lawsuit may argue, in the reasons section of their court papers, that a court decision is unconstitutional. The court said yes: if a decision is unconstitutional, a party may point that out while the case is still going on. The court declined to answer a second question because it did not explain how the views at issue differed from views already given.
raw.held: If a court decision is unconstitutional, parties may raise that in the reasons of their filings while the proceedings are ongoing. The second point raised could not be answered because it did not meet the Grand Justices' procedural rule (Article 4).

points.text: The question was whether parties may criticize a ruling as unconstitutional in the reasons section of their filings.
If a decision is unconstitutional, parties may point that out in their reasons while the proceedings are still underway.

The second point did not explain how the view it held differed from views already expressed by this body or other bodies, so it did not satisfy Article 4 of the Grand Justices Council rules and could not be answered.

who: Bodies that submit requests for interpretation

raw.answer: The case asked whether the first-term members of the Legislative Yuan and Control Yuan may keep exercising their powers when the nation faces a major crisis. The court said yes: if a major upheaval makes it practically impossible to hold the next elections under the law, the first-term members continue in their roles until the second-term members are elected and convene.
raw.held: Where a major national upheaval makes it practically impossible to lawfully hold the next election, the first-term legislators and control members continue to exercise their powers until the second-term members are lawfully elected and assembled or convened.

points.text: The Constitution sets terms of three years for legislators (Article 65) and six years for control members (Article 93), and a term would normally run from taking office until the constitutional period ends.
A major national upheaval can make it practically impossible to hold the next election according to law.
Letting the two Yuans' powers stall would clearly conflict with the Constitution's basic purpose of establishing a five-Yuan system.
So until the second-term members are lawfully elected and convened, the first-term members should keep exercising their powers.

raw.answer: The case asked how an interested party can object to a trademark that has already been approved for registration. The court said that if the party files its own application for a same or similar mark within the six-month public notice period and claims it used its mark first without interruption, the objection must be handled under the objection procedure and Article 3 of the Trademark Law.
raw.held: An interested party who, during the six-month notice period after approval, applies to register a same or similar mark and objects on the ground of earlier uninterrupted actual use must have the objection handled under the objection procedure and Article 3 of the Trademark Law.

points.text: Article 3 says that when two or more people apply to register the same or a similar mark for the same goods, priority goes to whoever actually used it first in the Republic of China without interruption.
Earliest uninterrupted use is the substantive standard for deciding whether to approve or reject a registration.

An interested party may file its own application for a same or similar mark during the six-month notice period after approval under Article 26 and object to the other's approved mark on the basis of its earlier, uninterrupted use.
Such an objection should therefore be handled under the objection procedure and Article 3.

who: Applicants for same or similar marks

raw.answer: The case asked whether the deputy representative of our country on the United Nations Korea Commission counts as an "official" (官吏). The court decided that this person does count as an official under Article 75 of the Constitution.
raw.held: The court held that the deputy representative is an official as meant in Article 75 of the Constitution, because the government appointed the person and set a one-year term, whether the body is temporary or permanent.

points.text: The deputy representative was appointed by the government.
The post has a fixed term of one year.
Whether the Commission is temporary or permanent does not change the result.

who: Deputy representative on the UN Korea Commission

raw.answer: The case asked whether, after the Constitution took effect, the secretaries-general (書記長) of political parties' offices were public officials. The court decided they should not be regarded as public officials. The paragraphs give no reasons for this conclusion.
raw.held: After the Constitution took effect, the secretaries-general of political parties and of party offices at every level may not be regarded as public officials.
who: Secretaries-general of party offices at all levels

raw.answer: The question was whether a member of the Control Yuan (a supervisory member) may also serve as a compiler at the National Institute for Compilation and Translation. The court decided that this post counts as a public office under the Institute's organization rules, so a supervisory member may not hold it at the same time.
raw.held: The compiler position at the National Institute for Compilation and Translation is a public office, and under Article 103 of the Constitution a Control Yuan member may not hold it concurrently.

points.text: Under the Institute's organization regulations, the compiler position is a public office.
Article 103 of the Constitution bars Control Yuan members from holding such an office at the same time.

who: Compilers at the National Institute for Compilation and Translation

raw.answer: The case asked whether an official document in which a government agency imposes a monetary fine can be used as the basis for compulsory enforcement. The court decided that it can only if a law provides that the document is sent to a court for enforcement or may be transferred to a court to handle. Otherwise, it cannot be used directly for compulsory enforcement.
raw.held: Compulsory enforcement against a person's property requires one of the enforcement bases listed in Article 4 of the Compulsory Enforcement Act. An agency's fine document counts as one under item 6 only if a law provides for sending it to a court for enforcement or allows its transfer to a court; otherwise it cannot be directly enforced.

points.text: Compulsory enforcement against a person's property cannot be carried out unless there is an enforcement basis listed in Article 4 of the Compulsory Enforcement Act.
An agency's lawful fine document can count as the enforcement basis in Article 4, item 6, if a law provides that it is sent to a court for enforcement or may be transferred to a court to handle.
Without such a legal provision, the fine document cannot be used directly to carry out compulsory enforcement.

raw.answer: The case asked whether Article 17 of the Pawnshop Management Rules conflicts with Article 949 of the Civil Code. The court decided that it does not conflict. It reasoned that pawnshops are officially supervised and open for business, so they should generally be protected when they take items in pawn.
raw.held: Pawnshops that take pawned items are protected by law, unless they knowingly accepted stolen goods. Article 17 of the Pawnshop Management Rules does not conflict with Article 949 of the Civil Code.

points.text: Pawnshops are supervised by the authorities and operate openly, so what they accept in pawn should be legally protected unless they knowingly took stolen goods.
Article 17 of the rules aims to balance the interests of the person who can claim an item back and the good-faith possessor.
Because Article 17 fits the spirit of Article 950 of the Civil Code, it does not raise a conflict with Article 949.

who: People who can claim back lost or stolen items

raw.answer: The case asked whether a person who adopts someone and at the same time marries that person to his own daughter is restricted by Article 983 of the Civil Code. The court decided that in this situation, a custom described as 'raising a son-in-law' (將女抱男), the restriction does not apply, because the two have no blood relationship by birth.
raw.held: When Person A adopts Person C and at the same time marries his daughter to C, Article 983 of the Civil Code does not restrict this, since the two have no biological blood relationship.

points.text: The adopted man and the daughter had no biological blood relationship with each other to begin with.
Because of that, the arrangement is not subject to the limit in Article 983 of the Civil Code.

who: Adoptive parents who also marry their daughter to the adoptee
Adopted persons married to the adoptive parents' daughter
Daughters married to an adopted person

raw.answer: The case asked whether a wife who, after marrying, goes back to her parents' home and does not return to live with her husband counts as 'malicious desertion' under Article 1052, item 5 of the Civil Code. The court said that on the facts described, where the husband repeatedly asked her through others to come home and she ignored him, it is hard to call this malicious desertion under that provision. It added that a spouse who still refuses to live together after a final court judgment ordering cohabitation, with no proper reason, may be treated by a court as falling under that item.
raw.held: A spouse who visits her parents after marriage and does not return, ignoring repeated invitations, cannot readily be said to have maliciously deserted the other under Article 1052, item 5. However, continuing to refuse cohabitation after a final cohabitation judgment, without a proper reason, can be found by a court to fit that item.

points.text: A past resolution lets agencies ask for an interpretation when they doubt a pre-constitution Judicial Yuan interpretation, and the Supreme Court doubted Interpretation Yuan-Tzu No. 750, so the court had to answer.

If a spouse still fails to live together after a final cohabitation judgment, and the situation continues with no proper reason why they cannot live together, a court may treat it as fitting Article 1052, item 5.
In the case described, the wife did not return after visiting her parents despite repeated requests, but this is hard to label outright as malicious desertion under that provision.

raw.answer: The case asked how to count the "90 days before the President's term ends" in Article 29 of the Constitution, which is when the National Assembly must meet. The court said the count starts from the day before the term ends and must reach a full ninety days. It applied this to the first President, who took office on 20 May 1948 and whose term ends on 20 May 1954.
raw.held: The "ninety days before the President's term ends" is counted from the day before the term ends, and the count must add up to a full ninety days.

points.text: The Constitution sets the President's term at six years (Article 47).
Article 29 says the National Assembly meets ninety days before each President's term ends.
The first President took office on 20 May 1948, so the term ends on 20 May 1954.
The ninety days are counted from the day before the term ends, until a full ninety days is reached.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the income of a public enterprise should be based on what the tax collection agency assesses or on what the Audit Department finalizes. The court decided that the Audit Department has the final say on the final accounts that agencies submit. If the two figures differ, the Audit Department's figure in the final accounts is used.
raw.held: The Audit Department has final authority to audit the final accounts agencies submit. If the collection agency's assessment of a public enterprise's income differs from the Audit Department's audited profit for the same enterprise, the audited figure in the final accounts controls.

points.text: The Audit Department has final authority to audit the final accounts that agencies send in.

So when the collection agency's assessed income for a public enterprise differs from the Audit Department's audited profit for it, the figure in the final accounts audited by the Audit Department is used.

raw.answer: The case asked whether civil servants may also serve as the president or other staff of newspapers and similar publications. The court decided they may not. It said that because civil servants already cannot be editors or publishers of newspapers and magazines, they also cannot be presidents (社長), managers, reporters or other staff.
raw.held: Civil servants may not hold the posts of president, manager, reporter or other staff member at newspapers and magazines, in addition to the editor and publisher posts already barred.

points.text: An earlier interpretation, No. 6, already held that civil servants cannot be editors or publishers of newspapers and magazines.
Under Article 14, paragraph 1 of the Civil Servants Service Act, the same bar naturally extends to presidents, managers, reporters and other staff.

raw.answer: This ruling dealt with two questions: what it means that judges decide cases 'according to law', and whether a county council can pass rules limiting people's freedoms and rights. The court said judges are protected from interference and may rely on valid rules other than statutes, and that a county council needs a basis in the Constitution or another law before limiting people's freedoms and rights.
raw.held: Article 80 of the Constitution protects judges' independent adjudication from any interference. 'According to law' means law is the main basis for judging, but judges need not ignore other valid regulations that do not conflict with the Constitution or laws. A county council acting in its legislative role may not restrict people's freedoms and rights without a basis in the Constitution or another law.

points.text: Article 80 of the Constitution is meant to protect judges so they can decide cases independently without any interference.
'According to law' means law is the main basis for a judge's decision.
It does not mean judges must reject every other valid regulation that does not conflict with the Constitution or laws.
A county council exercising its legislative power may not limit people's freedoms and rights unless the Constitution or another law supports it.

who: People whose freedoms and rights could be limited

raw.answer: The case asked whether members of the Control Yuan (監察委員) and Legislative Yuan (立法委員) may also hold paid civil or military posts. The court decided that directors, supervisors and general managers of publicly run enterprises are covered by the same civil service rules as paid civil and military officials, so they count as public office. Control Yuan members and legislators therefore may not hold those posts at the same time.
raw.held: Directors, supervisors and general managers of public enterprises fall within the 'public office and officials' referred to in Articles 103 and 75 of the Constitution. Control Yuan members and legislators may not hold those posts concurrently.

points.text: Directors, supervisors and general managers of public enterprises, like paid civil and military officials, are all subject to the Civil Service Act (公務員服務法).
Because of this, they fall within the 'public office' and 'officials' mentioned in Articles 103 and 75 of the Constitution.
As a result, Control Yuan members and legislators cannot also serve in these positions.

who: Directors and supervisors of public enterprises

raw.answer: The case asked whether an administrative agency may directly seize and enforce against the property of someone who refuses to pay a fine it imposed. The court decided that it may not. Fines must be sent to a court for enforcement as the law provides.
raw.held: After the Compulsory Enforcement Act took effect, only courts may carry out compulsory enforcement. Administrative fines may not be enforced directly against a refusing person's property unless the matter is transferred to a court as the law provides, and the earlier Yuan Interpretation No. 3308 still applies.

points.text: Since the Compulsory Enforcement Act took effect, compulsory enforcement can be carried out only by a court.
So an administrative agency cannot directly enforce against the property of someone who refuses to pay a fine; the fine must be transferred to a court as the law provides.
The earlier Yuan Interpretation No. 3308 remains applicable.

who: People who refuse to pay fines

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Control Yuan can propose bills to the Legislative Yuan on matters it is in charge of. The Constitution does not say so expressly, but it does say the Examination Yuan can. The court decided that the Control Yuan can propose such bills, and that this fits the spirit of the Constitution.
raw.held: The Control Yuan may submit bills to the Legislative Yuan on matters within its own responsibility, which is consistent with the spirit of the Constitution.

points.text: The Latin maxims that what is left out was meant to be left out do not always apply. They fail where the text has an evident gap or can be interpreted, and the Constitution has gaps, such as saying nothing about a law for electing Control Yuan members.

The drafting history shows that the heads of the other yuans were meant to attend the Legislative Yuan on bills in their areas, and that all yuans could propose bills. No delegate objected, and no special reason was given for letting only the Examination Yuan do so.

The five yuans are equal, each acting independently as a highest state organ within its own sphere. The Control Yuan and the Judicial Yuan need to propose bills just as the Examination Yuan does, so there is no reason to think they were deliberately excluded.
Only the Legislative Yuan votes on bills, but the other yuans know their own fields better. Letting them propose bills offers legislative input and is consistent with reason and law.
Since the Examination Yuan may propose bills under Article 87, the principle of equal separate powers and the drafting history of Articles 87 and 71 support the Control Yuan having the same ability.

raw.answer: The case asked whether the right to take back deposited items (money or property placed with a court) is subject to a time limit. The court said that when case money that should be returned to parties goes unclaimed after notice, the court keeps it and tries to return it. Because the deposit rules set no time rule for taking it back, the limitation period in Article 125 of the Civil Code applies.
raw.held: The right to take back deposited items is limited by the extinctive prescription rule in Article 125 of the Civil Code, because the deposit law has no provision of its own on it.

points.text: The question was whether the right to reclaim deposited items is subject to a time-limit rule.
Under an earlier interpretation (院解字第三二三九號), unclaimed money that should be returned to parties, after summons and a deadline notice, is kept by the court, which should try to return it.
The deposit law has no provision on this right to take back deposited items.
So the right is limited by the extinctive prescription rule in Article 125 of the Civil Code.

who: Parties owed return of case money
Persons entitled to take back deposited items

raw.answer: The case asked whether the old custom of taking in a boy while marrying a daughter to him counts as adoption, and whether an adopted child who later marries the adoptive parents' own child must first end the adoption. The court said that custom, where there is no blood tie, is really a marriage-into-the-family arrangement (招贅) and not adoption under the Civil Code. It also said that someone who was truly adopted and then wants to marry the adoptive parents' birth child must first end the adoption.
raw.held: The custom of adopting someone while marrying a daughter to him, with no blood relationship, is 招贅 and not adoption under the Civil Code. A person adopted as a child who later marries the adoptive parents' birth child must first end the adoption.

points.text: Interpretation No. 12's reference to the custom of 'taking a son in while giving a daughter' means cases where a daughter is married to the adopted person at the time of adoption and there is no blood relationship between them.
That custom is in substance 招贅 (a man joining the wife's family by marriage), and is not adoption as the Civil Code uses the term.
Where a person has been adopted as a child and later marries a birth child of the adoptive parents, the adoption must be ended first.

who: People adopted who want to marry the adoptive parents' birth children
Adoptive parents and their birth children
Families following the custom of adopting while marrying a daughter to the adoptee

raw.answer: The case asked whether a member of the Legislative Yuan can still hold the legislative seat after taking a government official post. The court said no: under Article 75 of the Constitution a legislator may not hold both, so one who wants an official post must resign as legislator. If they take the post without resigning, they are treated as having resigned at that moment.
raw.held: A legislator may not concurrently be an official under Article 75 and must resign to take an official post. One who takes the post without resigning is deemed to have resigned when taking office.

points.text: Article 75 of the Constitution bars legislators from also serving as officials, so they must resign the legislative seat to take an official post.
Taking an official post without resigning shows a clear intent not to keep serving as a legislator.
Because of that intent, the legislator is deemed to have resigned at the time of taking the official post.

who: People who take official posts while serving as legislators

raw.answer: The case asked what the word "public office" (公職) means in Article 103 of the Constitution. The court decided that the ban on holding other public posts in Article 103 is not limited to government officials. The paragraphs do not give the court's detailed reasons or say which posts count.
raw.held: The court held that the ban in Article 103 on holding another public post at the same time has a wider meaning than just government officials, unlike Article 75, which restricts only officials from holding concurrent posts.

points.text: Article 103's rule against holding other public posts is different from Article 75, which specifically restricts only government officials from holding concurrent posts.
Because of that difference, the meaning of "public office" in Article 103 is not limited to officials.

who: Holders of public posts covered by Article 103

raw.answer: The case asked whether staff of the Central Trust of China (中央信託局) count as public servants under the Civil Service Work Act (公務員服務法). The court said yes: the Central Trust is a state-run enterprise, and people serving there under the law are public servants under that Act. They therefore remain bound by the limits in the court's earlier Interpretations No. 6 and No. 11.
raw.held: Staff serving at the Central Trust under the law are public servants under the Civil Service Work Act, and they remain subject to the limits set in Interpretations No. 6 and No. 11.

points.text: The court accepted the request because an earlier resolution lets government bodies ask for an interpretation when they doubt a previous one. Here the doubt concerned Interpretations No. 6 and No. 11.
Article 24 of the Civil Service Work Act expressly applies the Act to all staff of publicly run enterprises.
The Central Trust is a state-run enterprise, so its staff serving under the law are public servants under the Act and stay bound by Interpretations No. 6 and No. 11.

who: Public servants under the Civil Service Work Act

raw.answer: The case asked whether the Taiwan Provincial Food Bureau (台灣省物資局), a government office, could bring an administrative lawsuit as the plaintiff. The court decided it could not, because only people (private persons) may be plaintiffs in such suits. The ruling also said a customs anti-smuggling provision does not give government offices that right.
raw.held: Only people may be plaintiffs in administrative lawsuits, so the Provincial Food Bureau, as a government office, cannot sue as a plaintiff, and the cited anti-smuggling article does not change this.

points.text: The Administrative Litigation Act, Article 1, lets people whose rights were harmed by an unlawful act of a central or local government office bring an administrative suit, so only people can be plaintiffs.

Under its organizational rules, the Provincial Food Bureau is an office under the Taiwan Provincial Government, which makes it different from the township self-governing bodies in an earlier interpretation (No. 2990), so that interpretation cannot be applied by analogy.
Article 32 of the Customs Anti-Smuggling Act has no special rule about who may be a plaintiff, so government offices cannot rely on it to sue.

who: People harmed by unlawful official acts

raw.answer: The question was whether the birth parents of a child who has been adopted out may file a criminal complaint on their own, for the child's benefit. The court explained that the earlier interpretations only looked at the adoptive parents' side of the family and did not address the birth parents. It added to them by finding no reason to exclude the birth family from the right to bring a complaint independently.
raw.held: The court supplemented its two earlier interpretations (院字第二七四七號 and 院解字第三零零四號), which dealt only with the adoptive family. It held there is no reason to exclude a child's natural blood relatives, such as birth parents, from the rule that a victim's blood relatives may file a complaint independently.

points.text: The court accepted the case for interpretation because doubts arose over its pre-constitution interpretations, which the Supreme Court's judgment relied on, and it answered under an earlier meeting resolution.
An adopted child and the birth parents and their siblings are still blood relatives under Article 967 of the Civil Code.
Adoption makes the child a constructed relative of the adoptive parents, treated like a birth child, but the natural blood tie to the birth parents continues to exist.
When adoption ends, what is restored is the mutual rights and duties with the birth parents. The natural blood tie itself needs no restoring.

Under the Code of Civil Procedure Article 582, birth parents may act in a lawsuit for the child when the adoptive parents' interests conflict with the child's. So birth parents can still protect the child's interests during adoption.

The Code of Criminal Procedure Article 214 lets a victim's blood relatives file independently, and there is no reason to exclude natural blood relatives. The earlier interpretations looked only at the adoptive side, so they needed supplementing.

who: Adopted children who are crime victims
